newsitem.title: ITALY: Lawyer calls for five life sentences for ex-Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer calls for five life sentences for ex-Nazis.

text.p: Former Nazi SS officers, Erich Priebke and Karl Hass, should be given five life sentences each for their part in Italy's worst World War Two massacre, a lawyer representing the city of Rome said on Tuesday.

Priebke and Hass are standing trial accused of complicity in the March 1944 massacre of 335 men and boys, who were shot in reprisal for a partisan bomb attack in occupied Rome which killed 33 German soldiers.

Nazi leaders demanded that 10 Italians should die for every one German soldier, but the SS got their numbers wrong and brought five extra prisoners to the execution ground at the Ardeatine Caves just south of Rome.
Although they realised their mistake, the SS decided to kill the men to eliminate all witnesses to the killings.
Rome city lawyer Giuseppe Lo Mastro told the military trial that Priebke and Hass should be given one life sentence for each of the five additional executions.

"Leaving those five witnesses alive would have shown who had carried out the massacre and how they had done it," Lo Mastro told the courtroom in Rome's high-security Rebibbia jail. "That was a risk the SS officers could not take."

Both Priebke and Hass have admitted shooting two victims each and Priebke also said he checked names off a list, but they argued they were following orders and would have been killed themselves if they disobeyed.
The proposed jail terms are the stiffest yet called for in the trial of the two Germans, both now in their 80s.
Last week military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano demanded a life sentence for former SS captain Priebke and 24 years imprisonment for former SS major Hass.
Intelisano said Priebke deserved the tougher sentences because his crimes were aggravated by cruelty, brutality and premeditation while Hass could claim mitigating circumstances.
Priebke, who was extradited from Argentina in November 1995 where he had lived openly for nearly half a century, is being held under house arrest at a Roman Catholic monastery.

Hass appeared as a prosecution witness in Priebke's first trial, which ended in uproar last August. A military court ruled that Priebke was guilty of complicity in the massacre but could not be punished under a statute of limitations.
Protestors besieged the court and Priebke was re-arrested a few hours later. The verdict was quashed on appeal.
Hass reluctantly testified at the first trial from a hospital bed after injuring himself while trying to flee from a hotel balcony. He was arrested after admitting he too took part in the shootings.
